docs.text: HardFOC core library RTOS Wrapper ¶ C++ classes for threads, mutexes, semaphores, queues, event flags and timers, over one C portability layer with a backend for FreeRTOS, ThreadX, CMSIS-RTOS2 and no RTOS at all. Quickstart API guide Source on GitHub HardFOC handlers and drivers need to lock, wait, sleep and run worker loops, and they must build for an ESP32 with FreeRTOS today, an STM32 with ThreadX or CMSIS-RTOS2 later, and a PC for host tests. This library gives them one API for all of it. Component code includes these headers and never names a kernel; a compile definition picks the backend. One API, one backend per scheduler Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your code uses the C++ classes (listed from include/ .h). Every class calls the C portability layer, the OS_ types and os_* functions of OsAbstraction.h and OsUtility.h, and nothing else. That layer includes exactly one backend header from include/os/, chosen by a compile definition (read from the table in OsAbstraction.h); with no definition the no-RTOS backend is used, for host tests and bare metal. The backend is the only code that names a kernel. Drawn from: include/*.h classes ; include/OsAbstraction.h backend table ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/rtos-layers.py . What you get ¶ Worker threads with a lifecycle. BaseThread runs Setup() , then Step() in a loop, then Cleanup() , and can be started and stopped again with verification. See BaseThread . Locks that work with the standard library. RtosMutex satisfies std::lock_guard and std::unique_lock . See Synchronization . Typed queues and event flags. OsQueue<T, N> with inline storage and OsEventFlags with WaitMode::Any / WaitMode::All . Timeouts are uint32_t milliseconds; UINT32_MAX waits forever. See Queues . Shared state without locks. hf::FlagsSaver , hf::SeqlockSnapshot and hf::ErrorHistory , each split into a reader and a writer interface. See Generic templates . Four backends, one contract. FreeRTOS (ESP-IDF SMP or vanilla), ThreadX, CMSIS-RTOS2 and no RTOS. See Backends . Host builds that keep time. The no-RTOS backend can take its clock and delays from your test harness, so timeouts expire without real waiting. See Backends . Used by ¶ Repository Uses hf-core-utils Carries this library as a submodule next to hf-utils-general and hf-utils-canopen hf-core RtosMutex in the handlers, PeriodicTimer , and BaseThread with the no-RTOS backend in the host build Where to go next ¶ Quickstart A worker thread in 30 lines. docs.text: Backends ¶ How a build picks the scheduler underneath, what each backend does differently, how to run with no RTOS, and how to add a kernel. Selecting one ¶ Define exactly one macro for the whole build (all sources that include these headers). OsAbstraction.h stops the build with an error when more than one is defined. Definition Backend header Kernel headers Core affinity Critical section HF_RTOS_FREERTOS=1 os/os_freertos.h freertos/FreeRTOS.h (ESP-IDF) or flat FreeRTOS.h , probed with __has_include Pinned to a core on SMP, plain create otherwise Spinlock on SMP, interrupt masking otherwise HF_RTOS_THREADX=1 os/os_threadx.h tx_api.h None (single core) tx_interrupt_control HF_RTOS_CMSIS=1 os/os_cmsis.h cmsis_os2.h None (affinity lives in osThreadAttr_t ) osKernelLock HF_RTOS_NONE=1 os/os_none.h None None No-op FreeRTOS is the backend in use today (ESP-IDF v5.5 on the ESP32-S3, FreeRTOS kernel 11.1). CMSIS-RTOS2 provides the C layer only OsUtility.h declares the os_*_ex helpers that the C++ classes call for HF_RTOS_FREERTOS and HF_RTOS_THREADX (and stubs them for HF_RTOS_NONE ). Under HF_RTOS_CMSIS the OS_* types and os_* functions of the backend are available; the classes are not yet. Capabilities that always exist ¶ os_thread_create_pinned and os_get_current_core_id are present in every backend. On a single-core kernel the first creates an unpinned thread and the second returns 0, so callers never need their own #if . FreeRTOS flavours ¶ Two families ship under the same name: Include layout. ESP-IDF installs the headers under freertos/ ; CubeMX and upstream ship them flat. The backend probes for both. SMP API. xTaskCreatePinnedToCore , tskNO_AFFINITY , portMUX_TYPE and the two-argument portENTER_CRITICAL exist only on multi-core kernels. HF_OS_FREERTOS_SMP gates them; the backend derives it from ESP_PLATFORM , portNUM_PROCESSORS and configNUM_CORES after the kernel headers are in. Running without an RTOS ¶ HF_RTOS_NONE=1 is for host tests and bare-metal images. There is no scheduler, so the kernel calls become stubs: Call Result on the no-RTOS backend Mutex lock and unlock, semaphore give and take, event-flag set, clear and wait Succeed at once OsQueue::Send() Returns true; nothing is stored OsQueue::Receive() Returns false Thread and timer create, start and stop Return true; nothing runs CriticalGuard No-op BaseThread::StartThreadAndWaitToVerify() Runs Setup() inline and marks the thread running ( src/BaseThreadHostStub.cpp ); you call Step() Build src/BaseThread.cpp , src/SignalSemaphore.cpp , src/RtosMutex.cpp and src/BaseThreadHostStub.cpp for a host build with threads. Time without a scheduler ¶ By default there is no tick: os_time_get() , os_get_elapsed_time_msec() and RtosTime::GetCurrentTimeUs() return 0 and every delay returns at once. Code that waits for a timeout by polling the clock then never times out. Define HF_RTOS_NONE_EXTERNAL_CLOCK=1 to take time from the integrator, who then provides two C functions: uint64_t hf_os_none_clock_us ( void ); /* monotonic microseconds */ void hf_os_none_delay_us ( uint64_t ); /* let that much time pass */ The hf-core host build backs them with a fake clock that advances on every delay, so timeouts expire without real waiting. One tick is one millisecond, the same as os_convert_msec_to_delay_ticks() on this backend. A bare-metal image can back them with a hardware timer. The porting contract ¶ A backend owns every kernel difference. A consumer build must never force-include a compatibility header, redefine a kernel macro or synthesise an include directory to make a backend compile. If a kernel variant does not fit, extend its backend header. Build systems select a backend; they do not repair one. Adding a backend ¶ Add include/os/os_<kernel>.h implementing the whole OS_* / os_* surface. Copy the structure of os_threadx.h . Add the selection branch and the table row to include/OsAbstraction.h . Declare the os_*_ex helpers for it in include/OsUtility.h if the C++ classes are to build. Add storage to src/CriticalSection.cpp if the backend declares os_critical_mux . Add the row to include/os/README.md and to the table on this page. The layer figure reads the backend table from OsAbstraction.h , so step 2 updates it. Next: Integration .

docs.text: BaseThread ¶ A worker task with a fixed lifecycle, Setup() , Step() in a loop, Cleanup() , that can be started and stopped many times and tells you whether a start or stop happened. Purpose ¶ Every HardFOC service loop has the same shape: prepare, repeat a step at some rate, tidy up when told to stop. BaseThread owns that loop, the start semaphore and the state flags; you write the five methods that differ. Lifecycle ¶ stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Created: EnsureInitialized() calls Initialize() calls CreateBaseThread() Created --> Waiting Waiting --> Running: Start() / StartThreadAndWaitToVerify() Running --> Running: Step() returns N, sleep N ms Running --> Stopping: Stop() / StopThreadAndWaitToVerify() Stopping --> Waiting: Cleanup() On every start the task calls ResetVariables() , then Setup() (once per start), then Step() until a stop is requested. After the last Step() it calls Cleanup() and waits for the next start. Example ¶ #include "BaseThread.h" class BlinkThread : public BaseThread { public : BlinkThread () : BaseThread ( "Blink" ) {} protected : bool Initialize () noexcept override { // creates the task once return CreateBaseThread ( stack_ , sizeof ( stack_ ), /*priority=*/ 5 , /*preempt_threshold=*/ 5 , /*timeSliceAllowed=*/ 0 , OS_AUTO_START ); } bool Setup () noexcept override { on_ = false ; return true ; } // on a start uint32_t Step () noexcept override { // the loop body on_ = ! on_ ; // toggle an LED here return 500 ; // ms until the next Step() } bool Cleanup () noexcept override { on_ = false ; return true ; } // after a stop bool ResetVariables () noexcept override { on_ = false ; return true ; } private : bool on_ = false ; uint8_t stack_ [ 4096 ]; // no heap: the stack lives here }; static BlinkThread blink ; bool StartBlink () { if ( ! blink . EnsureInitialized ()) { // Initialize(): create the task return false ; } return blink . StartThreadAndWaitToVerify ( /*startTimeoutMsec=*/ 1000 ); } bool StopBlink () { return blink . StopThreadAndWaitToVerify ( /*stopTimeoutMsec=*/ 1000 ); } Methods you implement ¶ Method Access Called Return Initialize() protected Once, from EnsureInitialized() True when the task was created; call CreateBaseThread() here ResetVariables() protected At the start of every run True on success Setup() public Once per start, before the first Step() True when setup ran Step() public Repeatedly while running Milliseconds to sleep before the next Step() Cleanup() public Once per stop, after the last Step() True when cleanup ran StartAction() public, optional From Start() , before the task is signalled False refuses the start Methods you call ¶ Method Blocks Does EnsureInitialized() No Runs Initialize() the first time; returns whether the thread is initialised Start() / Stop() No Signal a start, or request a stop StartThreadAndWaitToVerify(ms) Up to ms (default 1000) Start and wait until the task reports running StopThreadAndWaitToVerify(ms) Up to ms Stop and wait until the task finished Cleanup() Suspend() / Resume() / IsSuspended() No Kernel suspend and resume of the task IsThreadRunning() , IsSetupComplete() , IsCleanupComplete() No State flags GetStackHighWaterMark() No Minimum free stack seen by the kernel ChangePriority(p) No Change the task priority CreateBaseThread() has a second overload with a core_id argument that pins the task to a core on SMP kernels (0 or 1 on the ESP32-S3; a negative value means no affinity). Single-core kernels ignore it. Memory and timing ¶ No heap in the class. The stack is a buffer you pass to CreateBaseThread() , usually a member array. The object also holds a SignalSemaphore (with a 40-byte name buffer) and a few flags. The sleep after Step() is an os_delay_msec() , which takes a uint16_t : return at most 65 535 ms. The delay counts from the end of Step() , so the period is the step time plus the returned value. A stop takes effect after the current Step() and its sleep. Size the stop timeout to the longest step plus sleep. Not copyable. One object is one kernel task. On a host build ¶ With HF_RTOS_NONE=1 , compile src/BaseThreadHostStub.cpp as well. There is no task: StartThreadAndWaitToVerify() runs Setup() inline and marks the thread running, and your test calls Step() and applies the returned delay itself. hf-core's host tests do exactly this. Next: Synchronization .

docs.text: No heap in the class. The stack is a buffer you pass to CreateBaseThread() , usually a member array. The object also holds a SignalSemaphore (with a 40-byte name buffer) and a few flags. The sleep after Step() is an os_delay_msec() , which takes a uint16_t : return at most 65 535 ms. The delay counts from the end of Step() , so the period is the step time plus the returned value. A stop takes effect after the current Step() and its sleep. Size the stop timeout to the longest step plus sleep. Not copyable. One object is one kernel task.

Generic templates ¶ hf::FlagsSaver , hf::SeqlockSnapshot and hf::ErrorHistory : shared state for status flags, the latest value of a struct and a history of errors, each with a read side and a write side. The shape they share ¶ Each template is three types in one header: a pure-virtual reader interface, a pure-virtual writer interface and a final class that implements both. Give producers a reference to the writer and consumers a reference to the reader; the type system then stops a consumer from writing. Template Reader Writer Concurrency Storage hf::FlagsSaver<Id, N> hf::FlagsReader<Id, N> hf::FlagsWriter<Id, N> Lock-free, any number of tasks (N + 63) / 64 atomic 64-bit words hf::SeqlockSnapshot<T> hf::SnapshotReader<T> hf::SnapshotWriter<T> One writer, any number of readers, no locks One T and a sequence counter hf::ErrorHistory<R, N> hf::ErrorHistoryReader<R> hf::ErrorHistoryWriter<R> Internal RtosMutex R[N] ring None allocates on the heap. T and R must be trivially copyable (a static_assert checks it). None is for interrupt context. FlagsSaver ¶ A set of on / off flags named by an enum. Set() and Clear() are one atomic operation each, return false when the flag was already in that state, and bump a sequence counter. A waiter can block until any flag changes. #include "FlagsSaver.h" #include "OsUtility.h" enum class SystemFlag : uint8_t { kReady = 0 , kFault , kCount }; constexpr std :: size_t kSystemFlagCount = static_cast < std :: size_t > ( SystemFlag :: kCount ); static hf :: FlagsSaver < SystemFlag , kSystemFlagCount > system_flags ; // Producers get the write side, consumers the read side. hf :: FlagsWriter < SystemFlag , kSystemFlagCount >& flags_out = system_flags ; hf :: FlagsReader < SystemFlag , kSystemFlagCount >& flags_in = system_flags ; void MarkReady () { flags_out . Set ( SystemFlag :: kReady , os_get_elapsed_time_msec ()); } bool WaitUntilReady () { flags_in . ClearWaitEvent (); // forget changes already seen while ( ! flags_in . IsSet ( SystemFlag :: kReady )) { if ( ! flags_in . WaitForChange ( /*timeout_ms=*/ 100 )) { return false ; // nothing changed in time } flags_in . ClearWaitEvent (); // re-arm before checking again } return true ; } Member Side Does Set(id, now_ms = 0) / Clear(id, now_ms = 0) Writer Change one flag; false when it already had that state ClearAll(now_ms = 0) Writer Clear every flag IsSet(id) Reader One atomic load Snapshot_(out) Reader Copy of all words, the sequence number and the last change time Seq() , LastChangeMs() Reader Change counter; the now_ms of the last change WaitForChange(timeout) / ClearWaitEvent() Reader Block until a change is signalled; discard a pending signal Re-arm the waiter On the FreeRTOS backend the change signal stays set after WaitForChange() returns, so call ClearWaitEvent() before waiting again, as the example does. The timeout is passed to the kernel in ticks without conversion; it is milliseconds at the 1 kHz tick HardFOC ESP32 builds use. The event group behind the waiter is created on the first WaitForChange() or ClearWaitEvent() . SeqlockSnapshot ¶ The latest value of a struct, published by one task and read by any number, without locks. The writer makes the sequence counter odd, copies the value and makes it even again; a reader copies the value and retries if the counter was odd or changed meanwhile. #include "SeqlockSnapshot.h" struct MotorState { // trivially copyable float speed_rpm ; float current_a ; uint32_t timestamp_ms ; }; static hf :: SeqlockSnapshot < MotorState > motor_state ; void PublishState ( const MotorState & s ) { motor_state . Publish ( s ); } // one writer MotorState LatestState () { // any number of readers MotorState out {}; ( void ) motor_state . Read ( out ); // returns the sequence number read return out ; } Member Side Does Publish(value) Writer Copy value in; one writer only Read(out) Reader Copy a consistent value out; returns the (even) sequence number it read Seq() Reader Current sequence: even when stable, odd during a publish WaitForChange(timeout) / ClearWaitEvent() Reader As for FlagsSaver Read() costs two atomic loads and one memcpy of T when no publish is in progress, and retries while one is. Two tasks calling Publish() at once corrupt the value: protect them with a mutex if you ever have two writers. ErrorHistory ¶ The last N records of something (errors, events), oldest first. A full ring overwrites its oldest record and counts the overwrite, so a reader can tell that records were lost. #include "ErrorHistory.h" struct ErrorRecord { uint32_t timestamp_ms ; uint16_t code ; }; static hf :: ErrorHistory < ErrorRecord , /*kCapacity=*/ 32 > errors ; void Report ( uint16_t code ) { ( void ) errors . Push ( ErrorRecord { os_get_elapsed_time_msec (), code }); // overwrites the oldest when full } std :: size_t CopyErrors ( ErrorRecord ( & out )[ 32 ]) { return errors . Snapshot ( out , 32 ); // oldest first } Member Side Does Push(record) Writer Append; overwrites the oldest when full; false if the mutex could not be taken Pop(out) Writer Remove the oldest Clear() Writer Remove all Size() , Capacity() Reader Records held; N Snapshot(out, max) Reader Copy up to max records, oldest first; returns the count Seq() , OverwriteCount() Reader Change counter; records lost to overwrites Every call takes the internal RtosMutex , so all are O(1) except Snapshot() , which is O( max ). Next: Utility .

docs.text: Queues ¶ OsQueue<T, N> : a typed, fixed-capacity queue for passing values between tasks, with millisecond timeouts. Purpose ¶ Hand data from a producer task to a consumer task without a lock of your own. Values are copied in and out, so T must be trivially copyable; the kernel queue is already safe for many producers and many consumers. Example ¶ #include <cstdint> #include "OsQueue.h" struct Sample { uint32_t timestamp_ms ; float current_a ; }; static OsQueue < Sample , /*kCapacity=*/ 32 > samples ( "Samples" ); bool Produce ( const Sample & s ) { return samples . Send ( s , /*timeout_ms=*/ 0 ); // do not block: drop when full } void Consume () { Sample s {}; while ( samples . Receive ( s , /*timeout_ms=*/ 100 )) { // false after 100 ms with nothing // use s } } API ¶ Member Does Returns OsQueue(const char* name) Creates the kernel queue Check IsValid() Send(const T&, timeout_ms = UINT32_MAX) Copies the value in, waiting for space up to timeout_ms False on timeout (queue full) Receive(T&, timeout_ms = UINT32_MAX) Copies the oldest value out, waiting up to timeout_ms False on timeout (queue empty) IsValid() True when the kernel queue exists Capacity() static constexpr N timeout_ms = 0 does not wait. The queue is not copyable. Memory and timing ¶ Construction is eager. The kernel queue is created in the constructor; check IsValid() once at start-up. Items are copied in 32-bit words. The item size passed to the kernel is sizeof(T) rounded up to a multiple of 4 bytes. Send and receive are O(1) plus the copy of one item. Send() copies the value to a local first. Use a T whose size is a multiple of 4 bytes on FreeRTOS The FreeRTOS backend creates the queue with xQueueCreate() on the kernel heap; the inline storage_ array is not used, and the queue length passed is sizeof(storage_) (bytes), not N . Because each item is rounded up to whole words, the kernel copies more than sizeof(T) bytes into and out of a T whose size is not a multiple of 4. Pad small types (wrap a uint8_t in a struct with a uint32_t ) until the backend is fixed. On the no-RTOS backend Send() returns true and stores nothing, and Receive() returns false. Next: Timers .

Use a T whose size is a multiple of 4 bytes on FreeRTOS The FreeRTOS backend creates the queue with xQueueCreate() on the kernel heap; the inline storage_ array is not used, and the queue length passed is sizeof(storage_) (bytes), not N . Because each item is rounded up to whole words, the kernel copies more than sizeof(T) bytes into and out of a T whose size is not a multiple of 4. Pad small types (wrap a uint8_t in a struct with a uint32_t ) until the backend is fixed. On the no-RTOS backend Send() returns true and stores nothing, and Receive() returns false. Next: Timers .

docs.text: Synchronization ¶ Locks, wake-ups, event flags and critical sections: which one to use, a compiled example of each, and what each costs. Class Use it to Blocks Kernel object RtosMutex Protect shared data, with std::lock_guard Yes Recursive mutex, created in the constructor RtosSharedMutex Many readers, one writer Yes Two mutexes Mutex + MutexGuard Lock a named mutex with a timeout, RAII Yes Mutex, created on the first lock SignalSemaphore Wake one task from another Yes Counting semaphore starting at 0, created on first use OsEventFlags Wait for any or all of up to 24 event bits Yes Event group, created in the constructor CriticalGuard Keep interrupts and the other core out of a few lines No None RtosMutex ¶ The mutex for new code. It is recursive (the owner may lock it again), satisfies the standard Lockable requirements, so std::lock_guard , std::unique_lock and std::scoped_lock work, and can be moved. Take() and Give() are aliases for code written against a semaphore-style API. #include "RtosMutex.h" static RtosMutex config_mutex ; static int config_value = 0 ; void SetConfig ( int v ) { std :: lock_guard < RtosMutex > lock ( config_mutex ); // unlocks at the end of the scope config_value = v ; } bool TrySetConfig ( int v ) { if ( ! config_mutex . try_lock_for ( /*timeout_ms=*/ 10 )) { return false ; } config_value = v ; config_mutex . unlock (); return true ; } Method Returns lock() True when locked (waits forever) try_lock() True when locked without waiting try_lock_for(ms) True when locked within ms unlock() Nothing RtosSharedMutex adds lock_shared() / unlock_shared() for readers; RtosUniqueLock<M> and RtosSharedLock<M> are RAII locks with an optional timeout. Mutex and MutexGuard ¶ A named mutex and its RAII guard. MutexGuard takes the mutex in its constructor, waiting up to the given time (250 ms by default), reports through the optional bool* whether it got it, and releases it in its destructor. #include "Mutex.h" #include "MutexGuard.h" static Mutex bus_mutex ( "Bus" ); bool WriteBus () { bool locked = false ; MutexGuard guard ( bus_mutex , /*maxMsecToWait=*/ 50 , & locked ); if ( ! locked ) { return false ; // another task held it for 50 ms } // talk to the bus return true ; } Mutex::Lock(ms) and Mutex::Unlock() are the direct calls. The kernel mutex is created on the first lock ( EnsureInitialized() ). SignalSemaphore ¶ A named semaphore that starts empty: one side calls Signal() , the other waits in WaitUntilSignalled(ms) . Each Signal() releases one wait. BaseThread uses one to receive its start signal. The name is copied into a 40-byte buffer in the object, and the kernel semaphore is created on first use. #include "SignalSemaphore.h" static SignalSemaphore data_ready ( "DataReady" ); void OnDataReady () { data_ready . Signal (); } // producer task bool WaitForData () { return data_ready . WaitUntilSignalled ( /*msecToWait=*/ 200 ); // consumer task } OsEventFlags ¶ An event group with a typed wait mode. Wait() blocks until the requested bits arrive ( WaitMode::Any or WaitMode::All ) or the timeout passes, and writes the bits it saw to its last argument. Check the bits as well as the result On the FreeRTOS backend Wait() currently returns true on a timeout too, because the backend's os_event_group_get() always reports success. Compare the returned bits with the ones you asked for, as the example does. With WaitMode::All FreeRTOS also clears the bits when the wait is satisfied; with WaitMode::Any they stay set until you Clear() them. #include "OsEventFlags.h" constexpr uint32_t kAdcDone = 1u << 0 ; constexpr uint32_t kEncoderDone = 1u << 1 ; static OsEventFlags <> sensors ( "Sensors" ); void AdcFinished () { sensors . Set ( kAdcDone ); } void EncoderFinished () { sensors . Set ( kEncoderDone ); } bool WaitForBoth () { constexpr uint32_t kBoth = kAdcDone | kEncoderDone ; uint32_t bits = 0 ; const bool ok = sensors . Wait ( kBoth , WaitMode :: All , /*timeout_ms=*/ 5 , bits ); if ( ! ok || ( bits & kBoth ) != kBoth ) { // check the bits, not only the result return false ; } sensors . Clear ( kBoth ); return true ; } On FreeRTOS an event group holds 24 usable bits (the top 8 are reserved by the kernel). The template parameter of OsEventFlags<> is unused and kept for source compatibility. CriticalGuard ¶ Masks interrupts (and, on SMP FreeRTOS, takes the backend's spinlock so the other core waits) from construction to destruction. Keep the guarded code to a few instructions: no blocking calls, no logging. #include "CriticalGuard.h" static volatile uint32_t isr_counter = 0 ; uint32_t ReadAndResetCounter () { CriticalGuard guard ; // interrupts masked until the end of scope const uint32_t n = isr_counter ; isr_counter = 0 ; return n ; } Memory and timing ¶ After the kernel object exists (constructor or first use, as in the table above), no call allocates. Every blocking call takes a timeout in milliseconds; UINT32_MAX waits forever, 0 does not wait. None of these calls is for interrupt context. Next: Queues .

docs.text: Timers ¶ PeriodicTimer : call a function at a fixed interval from the kernel's timer service, without a task of your own. Purpose ¶ Heartbeats, watchdog kicks, polling a status pin: short work on a fixed period. The callback runs in the kernel timer task, so it must be short and must not block. Example ¶ #include <cstdint> #include "PeriodicTimer.h" static void Heartbeat ( uint32_t arg ) { ( void ) arg ; // runs in the timer service task } static PeriodicTimer heartbeat ; bool StartHeartbeat () { return heartbeat . Create ( "Heartbeat" , Heartbeat , /*arg=*/ 0 , /*periodMs=*/ 500 , /*autoStart=*/ true ); } void PauseHeartbeat () { heartbeat . Stop (); } void ResumeHeartbeat () { heartbeat . Start (); } API ¶ Member Does Returns Create(name, callback, arg, periodMs, autoStart = false) Creates the kernel timer; starts it when autoStart False if already created or the kernel refused Start() / Stop() Activate or deactivate True on success Destroy() Stops and deletes the kernel timer; safe when never created True on success IsValid() True between a successful Create() and Destroy() The callback signature is void (*)(uint32_t) ; arg is passed to it on every call. The destructor deletes the timer. Memory and timing ¶ One kernel timer per object , created in Create() . The object itself holds a handle and a flag. The period is converted to ticks with os_convert_msec_to_delay_ticks() , ms * tick_rate / 1000 , rounded down: on a 100 Hz tick 25 ms becomes 2 ticks (20 ms) and anything under 10 ms becomes 0. Use whole ticks. The multiplication is in 32 bits, so keep ms * tick_rate under 2^32 (about 4.29 million ms at 1 kHz). Callbacks share one task. A slow callback delays every other timer in the system; hand longer work to a BaseThread or a queue . Next: Generic templates .

docs.text: Utility ¶ Small helpers: wait for a condition with a timeout, read time and sleep, start a group of threads together, and turn FreeRTOS codes into text. TestLogicWithTimeout ¶ TestLogicWithTimeout(func, expected, timeoutMsec, checkIntervalMs) calls func() until it returns expected or timeoutMsec passes, sleeping checkIntervalMs between calls. It returns true when the value arrived. BaseThread uses it to verify starts and stops. #include <atomic> #include "Utility.h" static std :: atomic < bool > link_up { false }; bool WaitForLink () { return TestLogicWithTimeout ([] { return link_up . load (); }, true , /*timeoutMsec=*/ 2000 , /*checkIntervalMs=*/ 10 ); } The check interval is passed to os_delay_msec() as a uint16_t . On the no-RTOS backend without an external clock, time does not move, so the loop never times out: define HF_RTOS_NONE_EXTERNAL_CLOCK in host builds that call it (see Backends ). Time ¶ Call Header Returns RtosTime::GetCurrentTimeUs() RtosMutex.h Microseconds since start, from the kernel tick (tick resolution) or the external clock RtosTime::MsToTicks(ms) RtosMutex.h Ticks, at least 1 for a non-zero ms os_get_elapsed_time_msec() OsUtility.h Milliseconds since start, as uint32_t (wraps after 49.7 days) os_delay_msec(ms) OsUtility.h Sleeps ms (a uint16_t , at most 65 535) os_delay_time(t, unit) OsUtility.h Sleeps t in TIME_UNIT_US , TIME_UNIT_MS or TIME_UNIT_S #include <cstdint> #include "OsUtility.h" #include "RtosMutex.h" uint64_t MeasureUs () { const uint64_t t0 = RtosTime :: GetCurrentTimeUs (); os_delay_msec ( 5 ); return RtosTime :: GetCurrentTimeUs () - t0 ; } BaseThreadsManager ¶ Starts and stops a set of BaseThread objects together, named by an enum, with or without waiting for each to confirm. The enum must be unscoped ( enum , not enum class ) because its count also sizes a std::bitset . #include <map> #include "BaseThread.h" #include "BaseThreadsManager.h" enum AppThread : int { kControl , kTelemetry , kAppThreadCount }; // unscoped: also the bitset size static const char * AppThreadName ( AppThread t ) { return t == kControl ? "control" : "telemetry" ; } class AppThreads : public BaseThreadsManager < AppThread , kAppThreadCount > { public : using BaseThreadsManager :: BaseThreadsManager ; }; bool StartApp ( BaseThread & control , BaseThread & telemetry ) { static AppThreads threads ({{ kControl , & control }, { kTelemetry , & telemetry }}, AppThreadName ); return threads . EnsureInitialized () && threads . StartAllAndWaitToVerify ( /*waitToVerifyTimeoutMsec=*/ 1000 ); } Group Calls Start StartAll() , StartSelected(list) , StartAllExceptSelected(list) , and each ...AndWaitToVerify(..., ms) Stop StopAll() , StopSelected(list) , StopAllExceptSelected(list) , and each ...AndWaitToVerify(..., ms) Resume ResumeAll() , ResumeSelected(list) Hooks PreThreadInitializationActions() , PostThreadInitializationActions() (virtual, override in a subclass) The registry is a std::map copied from the constructor argument, so it allocates on the heap once; an internal Mutex guards it. FreeRTOSUtils ¶ freertos_ret_to_string(BaseType_t) and freertos_task_state_to_string(eTaskState) return a name for a FreeRTOS return code or task state, for logs. Without FreeRTOS they return "N/A (no RTOS)" . Compile src/FreeRTOSUtils.c with the FreeRTOS backend. Next: API reference .
